The California clingfish (Gobiesox rhessodon) is a small, intertidal fish that uses a modified pelvic sucker to cling to rocky substrates in the surge zone of the eastern Pacific coast. Comparative data from confamilial gobiesocids indicate a wet weight at birth of 0.0003 grams [Wwb = 0.0003 grams], a value estimated from the egg dimensions of the related Gobiesox strumosus, placing Gobiesox rhessodon among the taxa with the smallest hatchling sizes in the family. Such a diminutive starting mass imposes a high energetic demand for rapid early growth, as the newly emerged yolk-sac larvae must transition to exogenous feeding within a narrow window to avoid starvation. Under a stable water temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], the age at birth is approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days], a brief incubation consistent with the small egg size typical of the species.

Following hatching, juveniles undergo a period of rapid growth within the wave-swept intertidal zone, feeding on small invertebrates dislodged by surge. Sexual maturity is reached at a total length at puberty of 2.7 centimeters [Lp = 2.7 centimeters], a modest size reflecting the species' overall diminutive body plan. This early attainment of reproductive size is characteristic of small, short-lived intertidal fishes that must complete their life cycle within a physically demanding and highly variable habitat.

Adults of Gobiesox rhessodon ultimately attain a total length of 6.4 centimeters [Li = 6.4 centimeters]. The ultimate wet weight of sexually mature adults reaches 3.23 grams [Wwi = 3.23 grams], a body mass that is consistent with the allometric scaling relationship derived from the species' asymptotic length. This mass is attained gradually over several growing seasons, as juvenile individuals allocate energy primarily toward somatic growth rather than reproductive effort during their first year of life.

Longevity in this species reaches a maximum of approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] at the same reference temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], a considerable lifespan for such a small-bodied intertidal fish. This extended longevity likely reflects the sheltered, predator-limited microhabitat provided by rock crevices and tide pools, allowing individuals to persist and reproduce across many seasons despite the physically harsh conditions of the wave-exposed shoreline they inhabit.
